newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria president paints bleak short-term view.
newsitem.headline: Algeria president paints bleak short-term view.

text.p: The Algerian president, in a rare news conference, has given his 29 million people a rather bleak assessment of their short-term future, diplomats and commentators said on Sunday.
About 50,000 people have been killed in a four-year-old conflict pitting Islamic guerrillas against the government in Algiers and the economy is shrinking.
"He was realistic on things where he had to be, such as industry, which is a disaster area outside hydrocarbons," said one senior diplomat.
"And it would be extremely optimistic to say 'terrorism' will be ended in the next two or three months. Economic and social conditions are the key to solving Algeria's crisis."
President Liamine Zeroual on Saturday gave only his second news conference since coming to power nearly three years ago amid a bitter, continuing conflict against Moslem fundamentalists.
It came one week after he chaired a partly boycotted, disputed political conference, planning general elections next year, and a referendum on constitutional change this year.

He told journalists on Saturday that security had improved but "terrorism", Algeria's term for fundamentalist rebel actions, would not be ended in "one or two months", although 2,000 youths had given in their weapons and repented.
Nor would the problem of unemployment and lack of housing be solved in one or two years, he said.

Zeroual, relaxed and confident on state-run television, said Algeria had the means to kickstart its economy. But privatisation was not going ahead fast enough, with only 10 small enterprises sold off so far.
His government on Saturday appointed academic Abderrahmane Mebtoul, 48, to run a Privatisation Council to speed up sales.
"Businessmen are not going to invest until security is better," the diplomat said. "They have had a framework in place for quite a long time, and have only sold off one small hotel.
"But he was making a point meeting the local press, to get them on his side for future moves."

Zeroual said Algeria was doing all it could to speed growth "but we must be realistic". Some firms faced "problems of liquidity necessary to take charge of workers' social problems, and to improve output."
Algeria has been cushioned for years by oil and gas exports which earn about $10 billion a year, over 90 percent of foreign income, and by running up foreign debt of about $32 billion.
But debt repayments started to take more than total income in the early 1990s, and turmoil around cancelled elections dominated by Islamists, followed by violence, forced a rethink.
Debts have been rescheduled and Algeria is now trying to switch to a free market economy. But nearly three decades of state control have left problems.

Outside hydrocarbons, some 400 state firms are estimated overall to operate at only 35 percent capacity. They provide jobs for around 1.7 million which the authorities, already with 2.1 million unemployed, believe must be saved.
Zeroual said a survey showed many firms could get growth through restructuring, but he warned some were not viable.
Last week, official figures showed non-energy industrial production fell by 7.4 percent in the first six months of 1996, compared with the first half of the previous year.
